10.headline: Jack Reaches One Hundred; Bill Corrects His Mistake Backwards
10.issueTitle: The Door Opens for Jack, and Nate Finds the Key
10.deck: A door finally opens, a bench finally empties, and one man learns the wrong lesson perfectly
10.column:
Wonderland runs on one rule. Everything you are told to do is correct, and doing it correctly makes you the wrong size for the door.

Jack got through.

He had stood on ninety-nine career wins for three consecutive editions while other men reached past him and let it swing shut. He beat Bolek by 28.58 to do it, with the third-best score of the week, in a game nobody would otherwise have discussed. Ninety-nine to one hundred is the smallest step in FantasyWorld and Jack has been taking it since 2011. He is also, quietly, in first place, which is the part of the afternoon he will remember second.

Nate is two away and nobody is looking at him.

He made the case with 157.08 and did not leave a single usable point behind — a flawless lineup, the second-highest score in the league, and Daniel dispatched by better than thirty. Emptying the roster onto the field has been managed sixty-five times in more than a thousand manager-weeks on record. Nate has now done it twice in three editions, which is either a method or a very good run of luck, and he has not said which.

Bill, meanwhile, learned his lesson and learned it inside out.

Last week this column recorded Bill benching RJ Harvey while Harvey went off for better than twenty. This week Bill started RJ Harvey. Harvey gave him 1.8. Kimani Vidal, watching from the bench, gave him 20.8. A quarterback who had been reliably worth twenty a week produced 6.8 on top of it. Bryan beat him by 38.9, and Bryan has spent most of this season being the man who does everything right and gets nothing for it, so the accounts are at least moving in a sane direction somewhere.

Bill corrected the exact error he made, in the exact direction he was told to, and it cost him more than the original.

Mario collected on an old grievance. Jonathan Taylor, who abandoned him at the worst possible moment two editions ago, returned 55.6 — better than double what he has been worth all year. Mario put up 165.3, beat every man alive, and did it to Justin, who has spent this season being praised in this column for never wasting anything.

Justin wasted nothing again and scored 86.44.

There was nothing to waste. He lost to all nine men, took the week's low mark, and fell from first to fourth without making a single identifiable mistake, which is the Wonderland tax in its purest form.

Bolek takes the belt for leaving 29.58 points sitting idle in a defeat, one edition after being congratulated here for a perfect lineup. That congratulation is withdrawn. Eric/Blakey won again, a third time, and remains ninth, a man running very fast to stay precisely where he was.

Gabes lost and stayed third. Daniel lost and stayed seventh. The table barely moved.

The door was never locked. Jack simply became the right size at last, and Nate is standing behind him now, unremarked, holding the same key.

11.headline: Bill Locks Away His Best Man, Wins by Eighteen
11.issueTitle: The Assets We Kept in Safehouses
11.deck: A week in which the field was won by the men who deployed the least, and the finest operative alive was spent on nothing.
11.column:
Every intelligence service operates on a rule it never admits to: an asset kept safe is an asset wasted. FantasyWorld spent this week breaking that rule in every direction and being handsomely paid for it.

Bill did the worst of it and profited most.

He had Sean Tucker, who was ready, and he left him behind the wire. In his place he sent out Kimani Vidal, who came back with 1.7 points and, one presumes, an apology. Tucker sat out the entire operation and produced 35. This is the third consecutive edition in which Bill has correctly identified which of his men could do the job and then filed the paperwork the wrong way round, and it is now beyond accident. He finished the week with 47.1 useful points locked in a room he never opened.

He won by 17.92.

The man he beat had the finest operative in the league. Josh Allen gave Eric/Blakey 45.18, better than double what he has been worth all season, an afternoon that would have carried most men through most weeks. It bought him his eighth defeat. Eric/Blakey has now assembled a competent, well-run, thoroughly professional operation, and it has three wins to show for it.

The same transaction ran again one table over, with the participants swapped.

Gabes kept 34.9 points in reserve and beat Bryan by 2.34. Bryan sent out virtually everything he had, held back 4.2, and remains the most efficient manager in FantasyWorld at better than ninety-five per cent. He is four and seven. This column has argued for weeks that his method pays late and never enough. It has stopped paying altogether.

Daniel, meanwhile, ran the cleanest operation of the week and was rewarded with a place in the middle of the table.

He scored 142.52, more than any man in the league, left almost nothing unused, and beat Jack by 30.28 — his seventh win in nine meetings with him. Jack lost his grip on the top of the standings in the process. Daniel is seventh.

Nate is still two wins from one hundred and nobody has yet let him near them. He scored 117.9, which was fifth best in the league and entirely insufficient, because Mario put up 135 against him while receiving 3.84 from Justin Herbert. A quarterback who has been worth better than twenty a week simply failed to report, and Mario won by seventeen anyway and took first place. That is the fourth edition running in which Nate has been left standing outside the door.

Bolek keeps the belt, which he has now held for two editions and worn for three weeks in total. He scored the lowest total in the league, lost to every man alive, and did it with 27.2 points sitting idle in his own building. He is two and nine.

Four men are tied at seven and four and none of them earned it the same way.

FantasyWorld does not audit what you left behind. It only counts what the other man managed to get out of the field.

12.headline: Bolek Deposes Mario; Bill Executed for Doing Everything Right
12.issueTitle: Two Flawless Men, One Crown, One Axe
12.deck: Two managers emptied their rosters onto the field this week, and the court rewarded exactly one of them.
12.column:
Every court runs on a rule nobody says aloud: nearness to the throne is more dangerous than distance from it. The men at the bottom of this table have nothing to lose and no one watching them. The man at the top has both.

Mario found this out from the scullery.

He has been the strongest man in FantasyWorld since the season began, with more points than anyone alive and the power rankings held in an unbroken grip. Two editions ago Jonathan Taylor returned to him in triumph and produced better than fifty. This week Taylor came back from the field with 7.6, some eighteen short of what he has been worth all year, and Mario stood there holding him.

Bolek beat him by eight points. Mario had 16.3 sitting behind him, unused.

Bolek is three and nine. He arrived at this meeting having spent two editions wearing the belt for incompetence and handed it to Mario personally on his way out of the room. Mario fell three places in the standings in a single afternoon, which is the most any man has moved all season, and he did it while remaining, by every measure that is not the table, the best team in the league.

Bill's fate was worse, because Bill did nothing wrong at all.

For three editions this column has recorded Bill identifying his best available man and then benching him with real conviction. This week he emptied the roster. Every point he owned went onto the field — 122.38, not one left behind, a thing managed sixty-five times in more than a thousand manager-weeks on record.

He lost by 19.14 to a man who benched DJ Moore.

Gabes started Emeka Egbuka instead, for 3.7 against Moore's 18.9, hid nearly eighteen points in total, and walked away eight and four in third place. Bill has now been wrong at maximum volume and won, and correct to the last decimal and lost. He is welcome to draw whatever conclusion he likes; there isn't one.

The other perfect lineup was Justin's, and Justin was crowned for it. He put 137.68 on the field with nothing held back, beat Daniel, and took first place outright. He is also three wins from one hundred, and he is now the faster of the two men approaching that door.

Nate is two away. He has been two away for five consecutive editions. Jack beat him by better than thirty, only the third time Jack has managed it in ten meetings, and chose this week to do it.

Bryan, at last, was paid.

Jahmyr Gibbs gave him 51.9, three times what he has been worth this season, and Bryan posted the highest score in FantasyWorld and beat every man alive. This column has argued for weeks that his relentless efficiency pays late and never enough. It has now paid, once, gloriously, against the only man in the league having a worse year than he is. He is five and seven and eighth.

Eric/Blakey took the week's low mark, his third, and lost to all nine.

The court punished flawlessness and rewarded it in the same afternoon and did not trouble itself to say which was which.

13.issueTitle: Rations for the Man Who Spent Everything
13.deck: A week in which the disciplined starved, the careless ate, and Bolek buried thirty points in the dirt
13.column:
The first rule of a ruined world is that you carry nothing you cannot use. FantasyWorld spent this week obeying it, ignoring it, and discovering that the wasteland does not check your pack before it decides who eats.

Bill has now been punished twice running for doing everything correctly.

He went out with essentially nothing held back — 1.6 points left in the shelter, a rounding error, dust in the bottom of the bag — and Jack beat him by 2.22. Read those two figures in the order they occurred. The margin was larger than everything Bill owned and did not use. There was no lineup available to him, no reconsideration, no clever substitution, that would have changed the result. He was not outmanaged. He was simply out on the wrong patch of ground, and Jack took first place off the back of it.

Daniel spent the same afternoon walking confidently in the wrong direction and stumbling into a working well.

He sent Rome Odunze into the field and got 1.3 back. Terry McLaurin, who was standing right there and produced 18.1, was not asked to go. In total Daniel abandoned nearly thirty-nine useful points, posted the second-highest score in the league regardless, and beat Mario. He is now eight and three lifetime against the man, which is beginning to look less like a rivalry and more like a toll road.

Mario, for his part, has scored more points than any man in FantasyWorld by a wide margin and sits fourth with seven wins and six losses. Jaxon Smith-Njigba, worth better than eighteen a week to him all season, came back with 3.3. That is two consecutive editions in which the strongest operation in the league has been beaten while somebody less careful drove away with the supplies.

Bryan found the intact silo.

One hundred and fifty-eight points. The best score in the league, better than every other man alive, powered by a Seattle defence that has averaged a shade over ten all year and chose this week to produce 32.5. He beat Bolek by 47.36, which matters chiefly because Bryan had lost eight of their ten meetings before it. For weeks this column argued his efficiency paid late and never enough. It has now paid twice in a row. Both times against the two worst-off men in the league. He is sixth in the power rankings and seventh in the table.

Bolek reclaimed the belt one edition after handing it to Mario, having lost while sitting on 30.7 points he never deployed. In a season of three wins and ten defeats, that is not scarcity. That is hoarding.

The minor fates: Gabes survived Justin by 1.48 and holds nine and four; Justin dropped to third and remains three wins from one hundred; Nate finished 0.04 behind Gabes in a different fight entirely, lost his third straight, and stays on ninety-eight for a sixth edition; Eric/Blakey finally won one.

The wasteland does not reward preparation. It only notices who is still standing.

14.headline: Daniel Falls Fully Armed; Justin Fights Perfectly and Loses
14.deck: One man abandoned half a roster in the tunnel, another spent every point he owned, and the sand charged them both the same fee.
14.column:
The arena does not grade technique. It counts who walks back out through the gate, and it has never once asked a man what he left behind in the armoury.

Daniel left behind more than anyone has this season.

He sent Jayden Daniels onto the sand and got 3.22 back. Shedeur Sanders, who would have returned 35.96, stood in the tunnel the entire afternoon holding a weapon nobody asked him to draw. In total Daniel walked out of the arena still carrying 51.54 points he never deployed, posted the lowest score in FantasyWorld, lost to all nine men alive, and fell three places in a single afternoon to a man who is five and nine.

Last edition he did precisely this — benched Terry McLaurin, abandoned nearly thirty-nine points, and won anyway — and this column asked only whether the carelessness would catch him before the playoffs did.

It caught him in one week.

Justin died the opposite death. He went out with nothing held back at all: every point he owned on the field, an empty bench, a thing achieved sixty-five times in 1010 manager-weeks on record. It bought him 100.02 points, the ninth-best mark of the week, and a thirty-point defeat. He fought flawlessly and beat exactly one man in the building. He is still three wins short of one hundred, and he has now been stalled on ninety-seven for three editions.

The man who killed him is one away.

Nate spent six consecutive editions frozen on ninety-eight career wins. He has now taken two of them in short order and stands at ninety-nine, a single victory from the wooden sword, with the whole league watching the gate he has to walk through.

Bill, at last, was paid.

This column has spent five instalments recording a man who emptied his pack, did everything correctly and was beaten for it — once by a margin larger than everything he had withheld. This week he put 147.52 on the sand, the best figure in the league, and beat every man in it. He climbed four places in the power rankings. He is seven and seven, fifth, and scoring more than almost anyone. The reward arrived; the table barely acknowledged it.

Bryan won by 0.7.

He did it while Jalen Hurts, worth better than twenty a week to him all season, produced four tenths of a point and went home. That is a quarterback contributing nothing whatsoever, and Bryan still walked out, because he wastes less than any man in FantasyWorld and it finally billed the correct address. His previous two payments came against the two worst-off men in the league. This one came off the man sitting first in the table.

The minor fates: Mario got 33.2 from Puka Nacua, beat Gabes, and remains the strongest operation in the league at eight and six; Gabes lost and still holds nine and five; Jack lost and still holds first place; Bolek conceded thirty and stands three and eleven.

Daniel went out armed to the teeth. Justin went out with nothing to spare. The sand does not distinguish between them, and neither, in the end, does the standings table.

Every court runs on a rule nobody says aloud: nearness to the throne is more dangerous than distance from it. The men at the bottom of this table have nothing to lose and no one watching them. The man at the top has both.

Mario found this out from the scullery.

He has been the strongest man in FantasyWorld since the season began, with more points than anyone alive and the power rankings held in an unbroken grip. Two editions ago Jonathan Taylor returned to him in triumph and produced better than fifty. This week Taylor came back from the field with 7.6, some eighteen short of what he has been worth all year, and Mario stood there holding him.

Bolek beat him by eight points. Mario had 16.3 sitting behind him, unused.

Bryan found the intact silo.

One hundred and fifty-eight points. The wasteland does not reward preparation. It only notices who is still standing.

06.headline: Bryan Sails a Perfect Ship, Sinks Anyway
06.issueTitle: The Flawless Ship and the Cannon That Did Not Care
06.deck: A flawless lineup, the week's largest score wasted, and two captains creeping toward a hundred wins.
06.column:
There is no jury on open water. A man can trim every sail, stow every barrel, leave nothing loose on deck, and still meet a bigger ship coming the other way.

Bryan did everything correctly. Not one usable point was left in the hold. Every man he owned who could have helped him was on the field helping him, which is rare enough that it has happened only sixty-five times across the whole Sleeper era of this league.

He scored 105.96.

Justin came over the horizon with forty more and took the lot, his fifth win in a row. Bryan is now the most efficient manager in FantasyWorld at 94.7 percent, a figure that would ordinarily indicate a contender, and he sits eighth with two wins. He is not managing badly. He is simply sailing a smaller ship, perfectly.

Bill fired the largest broadside of the week and hit nobody who mattered. His 163.2 would have sunk every other man in the league — nine for nine against the field — and it bought him a third win, sixth place, and the ordinary status of a man who is exactly average. Mario, on the receiving end, posted the third-highest score in the league and lost for the third consecutive week, which is a difficult trick to perform. He also spent the week watching Puka Nacua manage 3.8 points, and he keeps the belt for the cargo he left unloaded.

Gabes made the error of the week and it cost him the standings. He benched Kendrick Bourne, who scored 18.2, in favour of Emeka Egbuka, who scored 2.9, and then lost to Daniel by rather more than the difference — so the mistake did not decide it, which is somehow worse. It merely made a defeat inevitable that was already probable. Gabes has scored more points than anyone alive in this league and dropped two places.

Daniel, meanwhile, is one win from a hundred.

He has been in this league since 2011 and has never stood this close to the number. Jack, who has quietly won four in a row and shares first place on record if not on points, sits at ninety-eight. Two men rowing for the same harbour, one stroke apart, neither able to slow the other down.

The minor fates: Nate took Bolek comfortably and is level at three and three; Bolek is one and five and has beaten one man all week in the all-play, which is the sort of arithmetic that follows a captain home.

And then Eric/Blakey, six defeats from six, the week's lowest score, and a second low-week charge on the ledger. What makes it cruel rather than comic is that he has been setting good lineups all season — better than most of the men above him. He is not mismanaging the voyage. There is simply nothing in the hold worth defending.

Six weeks in, this league is rewarding the wrong virtues with total consistency. The tidy ships are sinking and the sloppy ones keep finding wind.

07.headline: Bryan Draws Perfect, Career Best, Loses by 1.46
07.issueTitle: The Quickest Hand in the Territory, Buried Anyway
07.deck: On this frontier a clean shot guarantees nothing except that somebody faster was standing across the street.
07.column:
There is no law out here and no marshal coming. A man may do everything a man can do and still be outdrawn by a stranger with a slightly better weapon.

Bryan emptied his roster onto the street. Not one usable point left behind the saddle — the second consecutive week he has wasted nothing at all, which almost nobody in this league manages once. And what he brought was the finest score of his career, better than anything in seventy-six games on his record, a total that would have killed eight of the nine men who rode out with him.

He lost by 1.46.

Mario was the ninth man. He had spent three straight weeks scoring like a champion and losing like a stray, and he chose this week to finally hit something, beating the entire field and the one opponent who had also brought his best. It is worth stating plainly that Mario did nothing wrong and neither did Bryan. One of them simply had a point and a half more, and out here that is the whole of jurisprudence. Bryan is now two and five with four defeats running and the most efficient hand in FantasyWorld.

Gabes committed the comedy of the week, and he committed it twice, in opposite directions.

Last week he benched Kendrick Bourne, who scored 18.2, and paid for it. This week he learned his lesson, started Bourne, watched him produce 1.9, and left Travis Hunter and his twenty points sitting in the wagon. The same man, the same error, reversed. He abandoned better than thirty points and beat Nate by twenty-four, which is the frontier's cruellest joke: the punishment never arrives when the crime does.

Eric/Blakey has a win.

Six weeks he rode in and six weeks he was carried out, always with a tidy lineup and never with enough in it. Bolek supplied the mercy, arriving with the ninth-best score of the week and twenty points he never called upon, which is why he keeps the belt and why the winless arc ends with somebody else's name on it. Both men are one and six. Only one of them is going the right direction.

Bill's week belonged to Bo Nix, who more than doubled his own season average and dragged Bill past Daniel, while Daniel's Justin Fields managed 4.54 and helped nobody.

Which brings us to the two riders on the same road.

Daniel came into this week one victory from a hundred and left it one victory from a hundred. Jack, who has now won five in a row and sits alone in first, closed the gap entirely — he is also at ninety-nine. Fifteen seasons for each of them and they arrive at the same number in the same week, neither able to slow the other, both needing precisely one more.

The minor fates: Justin's five-week run ended against Jack and cost him first place; Nate lost to every man in the league in the all-play, nought for nine, and took the week's lowest score home with him.

Somebody crosses a hundred next week. The territory will remember which one, and it will not care how.

08.headline: Gabes Handed a Miracle, Posts Lowest Score in the League
08.issueTitle: The House Where the Door Will Not Open
08.deck: James Cook delivered the game of the season and it bought Gabes a defeat to the worst team in FantasyWorld.
08.column:
Every haunted house runs on one rule. The rescue arrives, works exactly as promised, and changes nothing.

Gabes got his miracle. James Cook produced 41.6 points, beating his own average for the season by better than twenty-five, the sort of afternoon a manager waits all year to be handed.

Gabes then posted the lowest score in FantasyWorld.

Nought for nine against the field. Beaten by every man alive in this league, in a week when one of his own players had the best day anybody had. The rest of the roster stayed in the walls, and better than twenty further points sat on his bench watching, which is now three editions running that Gabes has kept his finest work out of sight.

The difference is that this time the bill came. He lost by 8.82. For two editions the joke has been that Gabes is only ever punished when the punishment is free. That protection has expired, and it expired against the last man in the league.

Bolek collected. He left nothing at all behind — a flawless lineup, every usable point on the field — and it came to 104.08, the second-worst score of the week. Bolek has fourteen all-play wins against fifty-eight defeats and the fewest points in FantasyWorld. For one week he was perfect, and perfect was enough, and it cost a man in fourth place his standing.

Nate was perfect too, and it looked entirely different. Two editions ago he lost to all nine men and took the week's low score home. This week he emptied the roster onto the field, scored 143.96, and beat Bill by rather more than Bill could stand.

Bill was busy doing the reverse. He benched RJ Harvey and started Rico Dowdle, who returned 6.4 where Harvey returned 23.1 — one of the two was ready, and Bill chose the other. He left 26.84 points unplayed and lost by 28.56, which is the specific cruelty of the thing: even the flawless version of Bill loses this game. He takes the belt from Bolek for it, and takes it fairly.

Bryan finally got paid. For four editions this column has recorded a man wasting nothing and winning nothing; this week he brought 149.52 and beat Daniel with it. The debt is settled. He is three and five, which is what a settled debt looks like when it arrives late.

Mario scored more than anybody, beat the entire field, and has now led the league in scoring for three separate weeks. Justin took first place back without much fuss and pushed Eric/Blakey to one and seven, a record that no longer has anything to do with how the lineups are being set.

Which leaves the two men at the door.

Daniel came into this week on ninety-nine career wins and was beaten by Bryan. Jack came into this week on ninety-nine career wins and was beaten by Mario. Both remain exactly where they were, for the second consecutive edition, each with a hand on the same handle.

Neither of them is allowed in yet. Something in there keeps holding it shut.

09.headline: Daniel Reaches One Hundred; Gabes Bars the Door on Jack
09.issueTitle: The Hundredth Name, Spoken at Last
09.deck: A dormant tight end wakes at the worst possible moment for Bolek, and the league's most efficient man is punished for it again.
09.column:
A coven runs on one honest rule. The words must be said exactly, and saying them exactly guarantees nothing at all. Both halves were on display this week, and the second half did most of the damage.

Daniel has one hundred career wins.

He got there on the back of a tight end who had given him under four points a week all season, a familiar that simply would not wake, and who chose this particular week to produce 35.3. That was the whole of it. Daniel beat Bolek by 3.48 with the seventh-best score in FantasyWorld, and nobody is going to remember the seventh-best part. He has been gathering this total since 2011, and it arrived by three and a half points against the man in last place, which is precisely how these things get handed over.

Jack walked up to the same door and Gabes shut it on him.

For three editions this column recorded Gabes hiding his best work in the cupboard and being spared the consequences. This week he left a point and a half behind and put everything else on the table. It came to 148.54. Jack lost by better than forty, his second straight defeat, and remains on ninety-nine for a third consecutive edition. The man corrected his one persistent error and the correction happened to cost somebody else a milestone. Nate, at ninety-seven, is coming up the same road and nobody has noticed him yet.

Mario chose the wrong ingredient and paid the full price for it.

He had Alec Pierce, who was ready and returned 16, and he used Deebo Samuel, who returned 4.9. Jonathan Taylor, reliable all year, produced 7.2. Mario still scored more than all but three men in the league and lost anyway, by 15.3, with 25.7 points sitting unused beside him. He takes the belt for it, and he takes it fairly. He also still leads FantasyWorld in scoring and sits fourth, which is the arrangement he has been living inside all season.

The beneficiary was Eric/Blakey, who put up 161.18 and would have beaten eight of the nine other men in the circle. It is his second win. He is ninth.

And then there is Bryan, who has now made a religion out of getting nothing for doing everything.

He set a flawless lineup. Not one usable point left on the bench, a feat managed sixty-five times in more than a thousand manager-weeks on record.

It came to 101.06, the worst score in the league, and Nate beat him by 42.04. Bryan lost to every man alive this week and is now one and seven lifetime against Nate. Perfect execution, executed perfectly, worth exactly nothing.

Bill did the loudest thing of the week and gained the least from it. He scored 165.12, beat the entire field, and dropped Justin by thirty-five.

Justin is still in first place.

Somewhere behind all of it, Bolek has lost seven of nine and Bryan has done nothing wrong for weeks. The circle does not reward the careful. It rewards whoever happens to be standing there when the tight end wakes up.
